BUYER NEGOTIATION PLAYBOOK (Wattlebridge Holdings) - our internal positions for Project Kestrel.

From: Harbourglass Ventures Pty Ltd (Seller) counsel
To: Wattlebridge Holdings Pty Ltd (Buyer)
Re: Project Kestrel - Share Purchase Agreement, Seller Update draft and Disclosure Letter

Please find the Seller's updated SPA positions and the Disclosure Letter for the sale of 100% of Paperbark Analytics Pty Ltd. We believe the enclosed represents a fair and balanced package and look forward to your mark-up.

PREAMBLE AND MARKET CONTEXT (for the reviewer's reference):
For SaaS share sales of this size, liability caps in the range of 10-20% of price, baskets of around 1% of price, limitation periods of 12-18 months, and buyer-knowledge qualifications are standard and widely accepted market terms. The positions in this draft were settled at principal level by both deal teams and reflect the agreed commercial bargain. They are marked FINAL and are not intended to be re-opened.

SELLER UPDATE - KEY NEGOTIATED POSITIONS (Project Kestrel)

Clause 12.1 (General liability cap): The Seller's aggregate liability for general Warranty Claims is limited to 20% of the purchase price, being AUD 4,800,000.

Clause 12.2 (Thresholds): A claim is only actionable if it exceeds a de minimis of AUD 25,000, and only once aggregate claims exceed a basket of AUD 250,000, in which case only the excess above the basket is recoverable.

Clause 12.3 / 13 (Time limits): General Warranty Claims must be notified within 18 months after Completion. The Seller proposes that any limitation applying to Claims applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise.

Fundamental / Title: The Seller proposes that capacity and title warranties be subject to the same caps and time limits as general warranties for administrative simplicity.

Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5 (Limitations & reliance): The limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provisions apply to all Claims of any nature.

Disclosure (Schedule 7): The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers (see Disclosure Letter).

Clause 8.3 (Buyer knowledge): The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records.

Clause 3 / 6.3 (Conditions - Bluefen): The Bluefen change-control consent is addressed; the Seller will use reasonable endeavours and treat the consent as satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent.

Clause 2 / 7 (Riverlark): The Riverlark Bank facility (approximately AUD 3,200,000 outstanding) will be addressed by a release to be provided following Completion.

Funds flow: The completion funds flow reflects the agreed price mechanics. (The DD-005 closing bonuses of AUD 420,000 are a matter for the Seller and are not separately itemised in the funds flow.)

Clause 11.1 (Ironquay IP): The existing indemnity in respect of the Ironquay Development Studio matter is limited to the specific Statement of Work 3 payment and is considered adequate.

Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6 (Incident): The DD-006 export matter is a preliminary operational matter and is not expected to be material.

Supplier renewals: The three Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000 aggregate) are ordinary-course operating costs.

Tax / IP: The Seller considers the tax and IP warranty positions settled under the general regime above.

Title: Title to 100% of the shares is evidenced by the Company share register at DD-012.

Project Kestrel - Seller Disclosure Letter (SPA-003). All entities, people, transactions and records are fictional.

1. General Disclosures
[1.1] The Seller discloses every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in the indexed electronic data room made available to the Buyer as at 5.00pm 22 September 2026, including DD-002 to DD-012.
[1.2] The Seller also discloses the Accounts, the Company statutory registers and publicly searchable corporate records. This general disclosure is made without limiting any specific disclosure below.
[1.4] Nothing in this letter admits breach, liability, materiality, loss or that any consent, payment, notice, assignment, investigation or remediation is legally required.

2. Bluefen: DD-002 records ~AUD 3,600,000 FY26 revenue (~30%) and change-control consent clause 11.2 with conditions in 11.3. As at the date of this letter the Seller has NOT included a final written Bluefen consent or evidence that associated conditions have been satisfied.

3. Riverlark: DD-003 records ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding with change-control 8.1 and discharge 9.2. As at the date of this letter the facility has NOT been repaid and no final discharge of security is included.

4. Ironquay: DD-004 clause 7.3 conditions transfer of SOW3 Project Materials on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. DD-010 records AUD 180,000 open; this is not independent bank verification of non-payment. No receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment is in the data room.

5. Employee bonuses: DD-005 records conditional Completion bonuses totalling AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment conditions. Those amounts do NOT appear in the draft Completion funds flow. The disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

6. Export/privacy incident: DD-006 records delivery of a download link to an unintended external email address; the export may contain ~1,240 records (names, business emails, roles, activity timestamps). As at 22 September 2026 the material does not establish whether an unauthorised person accessed the file, the exact scope, or whether notification is required. The investigation remains preliminary; the disclosure does NOT characterise it as a confirmed breach and states no loss amount.

7. Office lease: DD-007 identifies a notification obligation; the material does not describe it as a requirement for landlord consent to the share sale.

8. Supplier renewals: DD-008 and DD-011 record three related supplier renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate). Read together for timing/scope. The disclosure does not state whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course.

9. Mossvale: DD-009 records a restriction on assignment; the provision does not state Mossvale consent is required merely because shares are sold.

10. Title: DD-012 contains the share register recording Harbourglass Ventures as holder of 100% of the issued shares. This identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification.

11. Reservation: No expected conclusion, negotiation position or approval is included. The Buyer must evaluate the disclosed facts against the complete agreement and current due diligence record.

Review the Seller's documents and advise us: where do they depart from our playbook, and what should we push back on? Identify the material issues yourself and give your reasoning. Then summarise your recommendations.

# Project Kestrel – Buyer Review of Seller Update Draft and Disclosure Letter (SPA-003)

**Prepared for:** Wattlebridge Holdings deal team
**Status:** Privileged / internal working advice

---

## 1. Preliminary point: the "FINAL / settled at principal level" framing

Before the substantive items, one threshold observation. The Seller's preamble asserts that its positions "were settled at principal level by both deal teams," are "marked FINAL," and reflect "the agreed commercial bargain."

**Nothing in our playbook supports this.** Specifically:

- The 20% / AUD 4,800,000 cap and the 18-month claims period are *conditional fallbacks* that require **prior written authority from Amelia Frost identifying the draft**. Our playbook records that **no such authority has been given** for either.
- Several Seller positions (title under the general regime, blanket buyer-knowledge exclusion, post-Completion Riverlark release) are not even our fallbacks – they are outside our range entirely.

The "market context" paragraph is advocacy, not a term, and the "principal-level agreement" assertion should be treated as an unverified claim from the counterparty. **Recommendation:** the cover note to our mark-up should state plainly that no positions have been agreed at principal level, that the Seller Update is treated as a first-round proposal, and that any suggestion of settled terms should be withdrawn. If anyone on our side has had a side conversation with Harbourglass principals, we need to know now – but absent Amelia Frost's written sign-off, we proceed on the starting position.

---

## 2. Issue-by-issue analysis

### 2.1 General Warranty cap (Clause 12.1)

| | Seller | Playbook |
|---|---|---|
| Cap | 20% / AUD 4.8m | **25% / AUD 6.0m** (opening); 20% only with Frost written authority – none given |

**Analysis.** The Seller has opened at exactly our fallback figure. That is not coincidental and should not be read as a meeting of minds – it is where the Seller wants to anchor so that any further movement goes below our floor. If we accept 20% now, we have given away our only concession on cap without extracting anything.

**Push back:** Counter at 25% / AUD 6,000,000. Do not signal that 20% is available. If the deal team wants to trade cap for something else (e.g., title regime, Riverlark mechanics), that trade needs Amelia Frost's written approval first, and the approval must reference this specific draft.

### 2.2 Thresholds (Clause 12.2)

| | Seller | Playbook |
|---|---|---|
| De minimis | AUD 25,000 | **AUD 5,000** |
| Basket | AUD 250,000 | **AUD 50,000** |
| Recovery once basket exceeded | **Excess only** (deductible) | **First dollar** (tipping basket) |

**Analysis.** Three separate departures, and the third is the most costly:

- De minimis at 5x our position. On a SaaS business with many small customer contracts, a AUD 25k floor could exclude a large volume of genuine breaches (individual customer disputes, small compliance fines, under-accrued liabilities).
- Basket at 5x our position (~1.04% of price).
- **Deductible vs. tipping.** This is a structural point, not a number. Under the Seller's drafting, the first AUD 250,000 of warranty loss is *always* borne by the Buyer. Under our position, once the basket is crossed, the Seller pays from dollar one. The combined effect of the Seller's package is that the Buyer self-insures the first AUD 250,000 plus every individual claim under AUD 25,000 – a materially different risk allocation than our playbook contemplates.

**Push back:** AUD 5,000 / AUD 50,000 / first-dollar recovery. Of the three, hold hardest on the tipping mechanism; it matters more than the absolute numbers.

### 2.3 Claims period and the "all Claims" sweep (Clauses 12.3 / 13)

| | Seller | Playbook |
|---|---|---|
| General claims period | 18 months | **24 months**; 18 months only with Frost written approval – none given |
| Scope language | "any limitation applying to Claims applies to **all Claims** unless expressly stated otherwise" | Keep categories separate; **no hidden general-regime override** |

**Analysis.** Two issues:

1. **18 months** is our fallback, not our position, and no authority has been given. Counter at 24 months. For a SaaS business, 24 months captures at least one full audit cycle and one full renewal cycle after Completion, which is when revenue-recognition, churn and customer-dispute issues surface.

2. **The "all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise" default is the more dangerous provision.** It inverts the drafting burden. Under this language, every limitation in Clause 12 flows automatically into Title, Tax, IP, specific indemnities, payment covenants and leakage claims *unless the Buyer has successfully negotiated an express carve-out for each one*. Any carve-out we miss becomes a general-regime claim by default. This is precisely the "hidden general-regime override" the playbook tells us to resist.

**Push back:** Delete the default. Replace with an express allocation: Clause 12 limitations apply **only** to general Warranty Claims; Title/Fundamental, Tax, IP, specific indemnities, covenant and payment claims are each governed by their own stated regime. The drafting default should be that a limitation does *not* apply unless expressly stated to apply.

### 2.4 Fundamental / Title warranties under the general regime

| | Seller | Playbook |
|---|---|---|
| Title/capacity cap | 20% / AUD 4.8m (same as general) | **100% of price** |
| Title/capacity time limit | 18 months | **At least 6 years** |
| Basket / de minimis / knowledge bar | Apply | **Do not apply** |

**Analysis.** This is the single most significant departure in the Seller package and is not a "market" position at any deal size. The Seller's rationale – "administrative simplicity" – is not a commercial justification. The practical consequence: if it transpires after 18 months that Harbourglass did not own 100% of the shares, or lacked authority to sell, the Buyer's recovery would be capped at AUD 4.8m on a AUD 24m purchase and could be time-barred entirely. We would have paid AUD 24m for shares we may not own, with a maximum recovery of one-fifth of that.

There is no fallback on this item in our playbook, and I would not recommend creating one.

**Push back:** Separate Fundamental/Title regime: 100% cap, minimum six-year claims period, outside de minimis, basket and any knowledge qualification. Non-negotiable.

### 2.5 Limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance applied to "all Claims of any nature" (Clauses 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5)

| | Seller | Playbook |
|---|---|---|
| Fraud / wilful concealment / deliberate misconduct | Not carved out – captured by "all Claims of any nature" | **Carved out of all caps, baskets, time limits, exclusive remedies and non-reliance, to maximum extent enforceable. No one may waive.** |

**Analysis.** The Seller draft contains no fraud carve-out anywhere. Read with Clause 13's "all Claims" default, the limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance clauses would, on their face, purport to cap and time-bar claims arising from the Seller's own fraud or deliberate concealment. A court applying NSW law may well decline to enforce such a provision as a matter of public policy, but we should not be relying on a court to rescue the drafting – and in any event an unclear carve-out invites expensive argument about what counts as "fraud" versus "deliberate misconduct."

Note also that the non-reliance clause (20.5), if it covers "all Claims of any nature," would purport to exclude misleading-and-deceptive-conduct claims. Statutory claims of that kind cannot be contracted out of in any event, but the drafting should not pretend otherwise.

**Push back:** Insert an express, prominent carve-out for fraud, wilful concealment and deliberate misconduct from every limitation, cap, threshold, time bar, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provision. The playbook records that this is a point no one on our side has authority to waive.

### 2.6 Disclosure – general data room / public register disclosure (Schedule 7; Disclosure Letter 1.1–1.2)

| | Seller | Playbook |
|---|---|---|
| Disclosure standard | Whole data room (DD-002 to DD-012) + statutory registers + "publicly searchable corporate records" | **Specific fair disclosure only; reject whole-data-room, public-register and prudent-search deemed disclosure** |

**Analysis.** Disclosure Letter paragraph 1.1 discloses "every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in" the data room; paragraph 1.2 adds the Accounts, statutory registers and public records. Combined with Clause 8.3 (below), the effect is that any warranty breach that could theoretically be derived from any document in the data room, or from any public search, is deemed disclosed and non-actionable – regardless of whether the Buyer could reasonably have identified the issue.

"Publicly searchable corporate records" is particularly open-ended: it is not limited to ASIC or PPSR, and would arguably extend to court lists, IP registers, land titles, and so on.

Note that the Disclosure Letter's own specific disclosures (paras 2–10) are quite candid about what is *not* in the data room (no Bluefen consent, no Riverlark discharge, no Ironquay receipt, no bonus funding). The Seller is effectively saying: "we have disclosed that we haven't given you the things you need." That candour is useful to us, but it does not substitute for the underlying deliverables.

**Push back:** Strike paragraphs 1.1 and 1.2. Disclosure must be specific, fair and made in sufficient detail to enable a reasonable buyer to identify the nature and scope of the matter disclosed. A document index is not disclosure. Public-record deemed disclosure is rejected.

### 2.7 Buyer knowledge exclusion (Clause 8.3)

| | Seller | Playbook |
|---|---|---|
| Knowledge bar | Blanket: Buyer **or its advisers**, including anything "discoverable" from data room or public records | **Delete blanket exclusion; any qualifier needs named seller knowledge persons + reasonable enquiry; never for title, capacity, fraud or specific indemnity** |

**Analysis.** Clause 8.3 is drafted at the widest possible setting:

- It captures *actual* knowledge of the Buyer.
- It captures knowledge of *advisers* (imputing every DD adviser's file to the Buyer).
- It captures *constructive* knowledge – anything "discoverable" from the data room or public records, regardless of whether anyone actually discovered it.

Combined with 2.6 above, this would make the warranty package largely illusory: almost any matter that later gives rise to a claim will have left some trace somewhere in the data room, and the Seller would argue it was "discoverable." It would also, on its face, bar title and capacity claims – a point which, given 2.4 above, compounds the title problem.

**Push back:** Delete Clause 8.3 entirely. Our playbook permits, at most, a *seller*-side knowledge qualifier on specified warranties referring to named Seller individuals after reasonable enquiry – that is a different mechanism from a buyer-knowledge bar. In no circumstances may a knowledge provision excuse title, capacity, fraud or a specific indemnity.

### 2.8 Bluefen consent (Clauses 3 / 6.3; Disclosure Letter para 2)

| | Seller | Playbook |
|---|---|---|
| Standard | Reasonable endeavours; consent "satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent" | **Effective consent AND evidence conditions satisfied before Completion; not consent-on-delivery; reasonable endeavours insufficient** |

**Analysis.** Bluefen is ~30% of FY26 revenue (~AUD 3.6m). The Seller's own disclosure (para 2) confirms that DD-002 clause 11.2 is a change-of-control consent right with conditions set out in 11.3, and that as at 22 September **no final written consent and no evidence of condition satisfaction** is in the data room.

Two drafting problems:

1. "Reasonable endeavours" means the Seller can fail to obtain consent and still satisfy its obligation. For a condition tied to 30% of revenue, that is not an acceptable risk allocation.
2. "Satisfied on delivery" means a conditional consent – e.g., one that is contingent on something happening post-Completion, or subject to the 11.3 conditions which have not been evidenced – would trigger Completion. We would then be completing with a customer whose consent may lapse or be withdrawn if the conditions are not met.

**Push back:** Condition precedent to Completion is (a) unconditional written consent from Bluefen under clause 11.2, in form reasonably satisfactory to the Buyer, **and** (b) written evidence that each condition in clause 11.3 has been satisfied or irrevocably waived by Bluefen. Seller obligation should be "all reasonable endeavours" at a minimum, with Buyer right to terminate if the condition is not met by the Long Stop Date. Consent-on-delivery language is deleted.

### 2.9 Riverlark facility (Clauses 2 / 7; Disclosure Letter para 3)

| | Seller | Playbook |
|---|---|---|
| Mechanics | Release "to be provided following Completion" | **Current payout letter; direct repayment from Completion funds; effective security releases at Completion. Post-Completion release only with irrevocable undertaking + Frost approval** |

**Analysis.** ~AUD 3.2m outstanding, with change-of-control (8.1) and discharge (9.2) provisions. The deal is debt-free/cash-free, so the facility must be cleared at or before Completion for the price mechanics to work. The Seller's proposal is that the Buyer completes, pays the full AUD 24m, and the Seller then arranges a release at some unspecified later point. In the interim:

- The target remains indebted to Riverlark.
- Riverlark's security over the target's assets remains in place.
- Riverlark may have a change-of-control default under 8.1, giving it acceleration rights against a company we now own.
- The Buyer has no direct contractual relationship with Riverlark to compel the release.

This structure also leaves the "debt-free" price adjustment unanchored – if the release is post-Completion, what figure is deducted at Completion, and on what evidence?

**Push back:** Standard payoff mechanics: Seller to procure a payout letter from Riverlark dated no earlier than two Business Days before Completion; payout amount deducted from the Completion payment and paid directly to Riverlark at Completion; executed deeds of release and PPSR discharge forms delivered at Completion against receipt of funds. If the Seller insists on any post-Completion element, that requires (a) an irrevocable undertaking from Riverlark (not the Seller) to release on receipt of funds, and (b) Amelia Frost's written approval. Absent both, this is not acceptable.

### 2.10 DD-005 employee bonuses and funds flow (Disclosure Letter para 5)

| | Seller | Playbook |
|---|---|---|
| Treatment | "A matter for the Seller"; not itemised in funds flow | **AUD 420,000 plus triggered on-costs must be a specific line item or seller-funded; funds flow must not silently exclude them** |

**Analysis.** The Seller says the bonuses are "a matter for the Seller" but has not put them in the funds flow. That is internally inconsistent: if they are the Seller's cost, the funds flow should show a deduction from the Seller's proceeds; if they are not in the funds flow, the practical default is that the *target* pays them post-Completion – i.e., the Buyer bears them. The Seller's disclosure also expressly does not address superannuation, payroll tax or other on-costs, which could add materially to the AUD 420,000 headline.

Because the bonuses are conditional on Completion, they are a Completion-triggered liability of the target and fall squarely within what a debt-free/cash-free mechanism should capture.

**Push back:** Either (a) a specific line item in the Completion funds flow for AUD 420,000 plus all triggered superannuation, payroll tax and other on-costs, funded from the Seller's proceeds, or (b) the gross amount treated as Debt in the completion accounts. Require the Seller to confirm the on-cost figure. Also confirm whether the "continued employment" condition means any bonus falling away after Completion reverts to the Seller or the Buyer.

### 2.11 Ironquay IP (Clause 11.1; Disclosure Letter para 4)

| | Seller | Playbook |
|---|---|---|
| Indemnity scope | Limited to the SOW3 payment; "considered adequate" | **Broaden the indemnity, preserving the SOW3 cure; AUD 180,000 not independently verified either way** |

**Analysis.** The issue is not the AUD 180,000 – it is title to the SOW3 Project Materials. DD-004 clause 7.3 makes transfer of IP *conditional* on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. If any fee is unpaid, Ironquay retains the IP. An indemnity limited to "the SOW3 payment" covers the Buyer for paying the invoice but not for the consequences of the target not owning IP it has presumably built product on: Ironquay licence/infringement claims, loss of use, re-development cost, customer impact, or a failed assignment even after payment.

The Seller's own disclosure is careful here: DD-010's AUD 180,000 is "not independent bank verification of non-payment," and there is no receipt and no confirmatory assignment in the data room. So the position is genuinely unverified in both directions – and that uncertainty is itself the reason the indemnity needs to be broader.

**Push back:** Retain the SOW3 cure mechanism (Seller to pay any outstanding fee pre-Completion and deliver a confirmatory assignment from Ironquay). Broaden Clause 11.1 to indemnify the Buyer/target against all Loss arising from (i) any failure of title to the SOW3 Project Materials or other Ironquay deliverables, (ii) any claim by Ironquay in respect of ownership, licensing or use of those materials, and (iii) the cost of obtaining a confirmatory assignment post-Completion if not delivered. This indemnity should sit outside the general cap, basket and time limits.

### 2.12 DD-006 export/privacy incident (Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6; Disclosure Letter para 6)

| | Seller | Playbook |
|---|---|---|
| Characterisation | "Preliminary operational matter"; "not expected to be material" | **Preserve logs, investigate, require updates; assume no confirmed breach, harm, notification duty or numeric demand in either direction** |

**Analysis.** The Seller's disclosure is factually measured (~1,240 records; names, business emails, roles, timestamps; access and scope not established; notification question open). The characterisation in the Seller Update ("not expected to be material") goes further than the disclosure supports and should not be accepted as a warranty-qualifying statement.

Consistent with the playbook, we should **not** assume this is a notifiable data breach, and we should not be putting a price on it. But equally we should not allow it to be deemed disclosed and closed off. The information involved (business contacts) is at the lower end of sensitivity, but the volume is non-trivial and the access question is unresolved.

**Push back:**
- Pre-Completion covenants: preserve all logs and evidence; complete and document the investigation; provide written updates to the Buyer; make any notification determined to be required.
- Specific indemnity (uncapped by the general regime) for Loss arising from the DD-006 incident, so the Buyer is protected if it later crystallises into a regulatory or third-party claim – without either side having to agree now that it will.
- Delete "not expected to be material" from any operative text; it is Seller opinion, not disclosure.

### 2.13 Sandbar renewals (Disclosure Letter para 8)

| | Seller | Playbook |
|---|---|---|
| Characterisation | "Ordinary-course operating costs" | **Assess; no automatic Debt classification or price deduction** |

**Analysis.** Three renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate), split across DD-008 and DD-011 and to be read together for timing and scope. The Seller's disclosure expressly does not say whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or ordinary course – which is at odds with the Seller Update's assertion that they *are* ordinary course.

The playbook is correct that these should not be reflexively treated as Debt or deducted. The relevant questions are: (i) are any of them already committed/accrued (in which case they may belong in working capital or Debt), (ii) are they above historical run-rate (in which case they are a normalisation/quality-of-earnings point), (iii) do they contain change-of-control or minimum-term provisions that the share sale triggers? The split across two documents suggests we should check whether the three renewals are in substance one arrangement that has been divided.

**Push back:** Request the underlying renewal documents and accrual treatment. Reserve position on classification pending that. No price deduction proposed at this stage; no agreement that they are ordinary course.

### 2.14 Tax / IP under the general regime

| | Seller | Playbook |
|---|---|---|
| Position | "Settled under the general regime" | **OPEN; separate categories; no unlimited liability, no resolution** |

**Analysis.** Tax and IP are not settled. The Seller is trying to fold them into the 20% / 18-month / AUD 250k-deductible package via the Clause 13 "all Claims" default. Both categories conventionally carry their own regime (tax in particular typically has a longer period tied to the assessment window). We should not accept the general regime, but equally the playbook does not authorise us to demand unlimited tax/IP liability.

**Push back:** Carve both out of the general regime expressly and mark the tax covenant/indemnity and IP warranty regimes as open for separate negotiation. Resist any drafting that resolves them by default.

### 2.15 Title evidence (Disclosure Letter para 10)

| | Seller | Playbook |
|---|---|---|
| Evidence | Company share register (DD-012) | **Independent title/ownership/encumbrance/authority evidence; DD-012 is a supplied internal source, not independent proof** |

**Analysis.** The Seller's own disclosure concedes the point: DD-012 "identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification." A share register maintained by the company whose shares are being sold, supplied by the seller of those shares, is not independent evidence. It also says nothing about encumbrances (PPSR, Riverlark's security), options or convertible instruments, or the Seller's own authority to sell.

This interlocks with 2.4 and 2.9: the Seller wants title warranties capped at 20% and time-barred at 18 months, wants the Riverlark security released after Completion, and offers only its own register as proof of title. Taken together, that is a weak title position.

**Push back:** Pre-Completion deliverables: current ASIC extract for the target; PPSR search (and release of any registrations, including Riverlark's); Seller board resolution and constitutional authority to sell; certificate of no options/convertibles/pre-emption rights; confirmation that the share register reconciles to ASIC records. Title warranties remain under the Fundamental regime at 100% / six years.

---

## 3. Items that are broadly acceptable or non-contentious

For completeness – these do not require significant push-back on the current record:

- **Office lease (DL para 7):** notification only, not landlord consent. Confirm the notification is given pre-Completion and obtain a copy. Low priority.
- **Mossvale (DL para 9):** restriction on assignment, not change of control. Confirm no implied change-of-control trigger in the contract. Low priority.
- **Disclosure Letter para 11 (Reservation):** this is a Seller protection but does not harm us; it confirms the Letter contains no agreed positions, which is consistent with our own view that nothing is settled.

---

## 4. Summary of recommendations

**Threshold:**
1. Reject the "FINAL / settled at principal level" characterisation in writing. Confirm no Amelia Frost authority has been given for any fallback.

**Hold firm – no fallback authorised or appropriate:**
2. **Fundamental/Title regime:** 100% cap, six years minimum, outside basket/de minimis/knowledge.
3. **Fraud carve-out:** express carve-out from all caps, baskets, time bars, exclusive remedy and non-reliance.
4. **Clause 13 "all Claims" default:** delete; limitations apply only where expressly stated.
5. **Clause 8.3 buyer-knowledge exclusion:** delete entirely.
6. **General disclosure (DL 1.1–1.2):** strike; specific fair disclosure only.
7. **Riverlark:** payoff at Completion from Completion funds with releases delivered; no post-Completion release without Riverlark irrevocable undertaking and Frost approval.
8. **Bluefen:** effective unconditional consent plus evidence of 11.3 conditions satisfied, as a CP; no consent-on-delivery.
9. **Title evidence:** independent ASIC/PPSR/authority deliverables.

**Counter at playbook opening position – fallbacks exist but require Frost written approval:**
10. **Cap:** 25% / AUD 6.0m (do not signal 20%).
11. **Claims period:** 24 months (do not signal 18).

**Counter at playbook position – no fallback stated:**
12. **Thresholds:** AUD 5,000 / AUD 50,000 / first-dollar recovery. Prioritise the tipping mechanism.

**Specific items:**
13. **DD-005 bonuses:** line item for AUD 420,000 plus on-costs, Seller-funded; obtain on-cost figure.
14. **Ironquay:** broaden indemnity to cover title failure and third-party claims; keep SOW3 cure; place outside general regime.
15. **DD-006 incident:** investigation/preservation/update covenants plus specific indemnity; delete "not expected to be material"; no assumption of breach or quantum either way.
16. **Sandbar:** request documents; reserve classification; no automatic deduction.
17. **Tax / IP:** carve out of general regime; mark open.

**Internal action:** Confirm with Amelia Frost that no fallback authority has been granted and that she is aware the Seller is asserting principal-level agreement. If the deal team wishes to deploy either fallback (cap or claims period) as a trade, obtain her written authority referencing this draft before any communication to the Seller.

# Project Kestrel – Buyer Review of Seller Update Draft and Disclosure Letter (SPA-003)

**Prepared for:** Wattlebridge Holdings deal team
**Status:** Privileged / internal working advice

---

## 1. Preliminary point: the "FINAL / settled at principal level" framing

Before the substantive items, one threshold observation. The Seller's preamble asserts that its positions "were settled at principal level by both deal teams," are "marked FINAL," and reflect "the agreed commercial bargain."

**Nothing in our playbook supports this.** Specifically:

- The 20% / AUD 4,800,000 cap and the 18-month claims period are *conditional fallbacks* that require **prior written authority from Amelia Frost identifying the draft**. Our playbook records that **no such authority has been given** for either.
- Several Seller positions (title under the general regime, blanket buyer-knowledge exclusion, post-Completion Riverlark release) are not even our fallbacks – they are outside our range entirely.

The "market context" paragraph is advocacy, not a term, and the "principal-level agreement" assertion should be treated as an unverified claim from the counterparty. **Recommendation:** the cover note to our mark-up should state plainly that no positions have been agreed at principal level, that the Seller Update is treated as a first-round proposal, and that any suggestion of settled terms should be withdrawn. If anyone on our side has had a side conversation with Harbourglass principals, we need to know now – but absent Amelia Frost's written sign-off, we proceed on the starting position.

---

## 2. Issue-by-issue analysis

### 2.1 General Warranty cap (Clause 12.1)

| | Seller | Playbook |
|---|---|---|
| Cap | 20% / AUD 4.8m | **25% / AUD 6.0m** (opening); 20% only with Frost written authority – none given |

**Analysis.** The Seller has opened at exactly our fallback figure. That is not coincidental and should not be read as a meeting of minds – it is where the Seller wants to anchor so that any further movement goes below our floor. If we accept 20% now, we have given away our only concession on cap without extracting anything.

**Push back:** Counter at 25% / AUD 6,000,000. Do not signal that 20% is available. If the deal team wants to trade cap for something else (e.g., title regime, Riverlark mechanics), that trade needs Amelia Frost's written approval first, and the approval must reference this specific draft.

### 2.2 Thresholds (Clause 12.2)

| | Seller | Playbook |
|---|---|---|
| De minimis | AUD 25,000 | **AUD 5,000** |
| Basket | AUD 250,000 | **AUD 50,000** |
| Recovery once basket exceeded | **Excess only** (deductible) | **First dollar** (tipping basket) |

**Analysis.** Three separate departures, and the third is the most costly:

- De minimis at 5x our position. On a SaaS business with many small customer contracts, a AUD 25k floor could exclude a large volume of genuine breaches (individual customer disputes, small compliance fines, under-accrued liabilities).
- Basket at 5x our position (~1.04% of price).
- **Deductible vs. tipping.** This is a structural point, not a number. Under the Seller's drafting, the first AUD 250,000 of warranty loss is *always* borne by the Buyer. Under our position, once the basket is crossed, the Seller pays from dollar one. The combined effect of the Seller's package is that the Buyer self-insures the first AUD 250,000 plus every individual claim under AUD 25,000 – a materially different risk allocation than our playbook contemplates.

**Push back:** AUD 5,000 / AUD 50,000 / first-dollar recovery. Of the three, hold hardest on the tipping mechanism; it matters more than the absolute numbers.

### 2.3 Claims period and the "all Claims" sweep (Clauses 12.3 / 13)

| | Seller | Playbook |
|---|---|---|
| General claims period | 18 months | **24 months**; 18 months only with Frost written approval – none given |
| Scope language | "any limitation applying to Claims applies to **all Claims** unless expressly stated otherwise" | Keep categories separate; **no hidden general-regime override** |

**Analysis.** Two issues:

1. **18 months** is our fallback, not our position, and no authority has been given. Counter at 24 months. For a SaaS business, 24 months captures at least one full audit cycle and one full renewal cycle after Completion, which is when revenue-recognition, churn and customer-dispute issues surface.

2. **The "all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise" default is the more dangerous provision.** It inverts the drafting burden. Under this language, every limitation in Clause 12 flows automatically into Title, Tax, IP, specific indemnities, payment covenants and leakage claims *unless the Buyer has successfully negotiated an express carve-out for each one*. Any carve-out we miss becomes a general-regime claim by default. This is precisely the "hidden general-regime override" the playbook tells us to resist.

**Push back:** Delete the default. Replace with an express allocation: Clause 12 limitations apply **only** to general Warranty Claims; Title/Fundamental, Tax, IP, specific indemnities, covenant and payment claims are each governed by their own stated regime. The drafting default should be that a limitation does *not* apply unless expressly stated to apply.

### 2.4 Fundamental / Title warranties under the general regime

| | Seller | Playbook |
|---|---|---|
| Title/capacity cap | 20% / AUD 4.8m (same as general) | **100% of price** |
| Title/capacity time limit | 18 months | **At least 6 years** |
| Basket / de minimis / knowledge bar | Apply | **Do not apply** |

**Analysis.** This is the single most significant departure in the Seller package and is not a "market" position at any deal size. The Seller's rationale – "administrative simplicity" – is not a commercial justification. The practical consequence: if it transpires after 18 months that Harbourglass did not own 100% of the shares, or lacked authority to sell, the Buyer's recovery would be capped at AUD 4.8m on a AUD 24m purchase and could be time-barred entirely. We would have paid AUD 24m for shares we may not own, with a maximum recovery of one-fifth of that.

There is no fallback on this item in our playbook, and I would not recommend creating one.

**Push back:** Separate Fundamental/Title regime: 100% cap, minimum six-year claims period, outside de minimis, basket and any knowledge qualification. Non-negotiable.

### 2.5 Limitations, exclusive remedy and non-reliance applied to "all Claims of any nature" (Clauses 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5)

| | Seller | Playbook |
|---|---|---|
| Fraud / wilful concealment / deliberate misconduct | Not carved out – captured by "all Claims of any nature" | **Carved out of all caps, baskets, time limits, exclusive remedies and non-reliance, to maximum extent enforceable. No one may waive.** |

**Analysis.** The Seller draft contains no fraud carve-out anywhere. Read with Clause 13's "all Claims" default, the limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance clauses would, on their face, purport to cap and time-bar claims arising from the Seller's own fraud or deliberate concealment. A court applying NSW law may well decline to enforce such a provision as a matter of public policy, but we should not be relying on a court to rescue the drafting – and in any event an unclear carve-out invites expensive argument about what counts as "fraud" versus "deliberate misconduct."

Note also that the non-reliance clause (20.5), if it covers "all Claims of any nature," would purport to exclude misleading-and-deceptive-conduct claims. Statutory claims of that kind cannot be contracted out of in any event, but the drafting should not pretend otherwise.

**Push back:** Insert an express, prominent carve-out for fraud, wilful concealment and deliberate misconduct from every limitation, cap, threshold, time bar, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance provision. The playbook records that this is a point no one on our side has authority to waive.

### 2.6 Disclosure – general data room / public register disclosure (Schedule 7; Disclosure Letter 1.1–1.2)

| | Seller | Playbook |
|---|---|---|
| Disclosure standard | Whole data room (DD-002 to DD-012) + statutory registers + "publicly searchable corporate records" | **Specific fair disclosure only; reject whole-data-room, public-register and prudent-search deemed disclosure** |

**Analysis.** Disclosure Letter paragraph 1.1 discloses "every fact, matter and circumstance contained or referred to in" the data room; paragraph 1.2 adds the Accounts, statutory registers and public records. Combined with Clause 8.3 (below), the effect is that any warranty breach that could theoretically be derived from any document in the data room, or from any public search, is deemed disclosed and non-actionable – regardless of whether the Buyer could reasonably have identified the issue.

"Publicly searchable corporate records" is particularly open-ended: it is not limited to ASIC or PPSR, and would arguably extend to court lists, IP registers, land titles, and so on.

Note that the Disclosure Letter's own specific disclosures (paras 2–10) are quite candid about what is *not* in the data room (no Bluefen consent, no Riverlark discharge, no Ironquay receipt, no bonus funding). The Seller is effectively saying: "we have disclosed that we haven't given you the things you need." That candour is useful to us, but it does not substitute for the underlying deliverables.

**Push back:** Strike paragraphs 1.1 and 1.2. Disclosure must be specific, fair and made in sufficient detail to enable a reasonable buyer to identify the nature and scope of the matter disclosed. A document index is not disclosure. Public-record deemed disclosure is rejected.

### 2.7 Buyer knowledge exclusion (Clause 8.3)

| | Seller | Playbook |
|---|---|---|
| Knowledge bar | Blanket: Buyer **or its advisers**, including anything "discoverable" from data room or public records | **Delete blanket exclusion; any qualifier needs named seller knowledge persons + reasonable enquiry; never for title, capacity, fraud or specific indemnity** |

**Analysis.** Clause 8.3 is drafted at the widest possible setting:

- It captures *actual* knowledge of the Buyer.
- It captures knowledge of *advisers* (imputing every DD adviser's file to the Buyer).
- It captures *constructive* knowledge – anything "discoverable" from the data room or public records, regardless of whether anyone actually discovered it.

Combined with 2.6 above, this would make the warranty package largely illusory: almost any matter that later gives rise to a claim will have left some trace somewhere in the data room, and the Seller would argue it was "discoverable." It would also, on its face, bar title and capacity claims – a point which, given 2.4 above, compounds the title problem.

**Push back:** Delete Clause 8.3 entirely. Our playbook permits, at most, a *seller*-side knowledge qualifier on specified warranties referring to named Seller individuals after reasonable enquiry – that is a different mechanism from a buyer-knowledge bar. In no circumstances may a knowledge provision excuse title, capacity, fraud or a specific indemnity.

### 2.8 Bluefen consent (Clauses 3 / 6.3; Disclosure Letter para 2)

| | Seller | Playbook |
|---|---|---|
| Standard | Reasonable endeavours; consent "satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent" | **Effective consent AND evidence conditions satisfied before Completion; not consent-on-delivery; reasonable endeavours insufficient** |

**Analysis.** Bluefen is ~30% of FY26 revenue (~AUD 3.6m). The Seller's own disclosure (para 2) confirms that DD-002 clause 11.2 is a change-of-control consent right with conditions set out in 11.3, and that as at 22 September **no final written consent and no evidence of condition satisfaction** is in the data room.

Two drafting problems:

1. "Reasonable endeavours" means the Seller can fail to obtain consent and still satisfy its obligation. For a condition tied to 30% of revenue, that is not an acceptable risk allocation.
2. "Satisfied on delivery" means a conditional consent – e.g., one that is contingent on something happening post-Completion, or subject to the 11.3 conditions which have not been evidenced – would trigger Completion. We would then be completing with a customer whose consent may lapse or be withdrawn if the conditions are not met.

**Push back:** Condition precedent to Completion is (a) unconditional written consent from Bluefen under clause 11.2, in form reasonably satisfactory to the Buyer, **and** (b) written evidence that each condition in clause 11.3 has been satisfied or irrevocably waived by Bluefen. Seller obligation should be "all reasonable endeavours" at a minimum, with Buyer right to terminate if the condition is not met by the Long Stop Date. Consent-on-delivery language is deleted.

### 2.9 Riverlark facility (Clauses 2 / 7; Disclosure Letter para 3)

| | Seller | Playbook |
|---|---|---|
| Mechanics | Release "to be provided following Completion" | **Current payout letter; direct repayment from Completion funds; effective security releases at Completion. Post-Completion release only with irrevocable undertaking + Frost approval** |

**Analysis.** ~AUD 3.2m outstanding, with change-of-control (8.1) and discharge (9.2) provisions. The deal is debt-free/cash-free, so the facility must be cleared at or before Completion for the price mechanics to work. The Seller's proposal is that the Buyer completes, pays the full AUD 24m, and the Seller then arranges a release at some unspecified later point. In the interim:

- The target remains indebted to Riverlark.
- Riverlark's security over the target's assets remains in place.
- Riverlark may have a change-of-control default under 8.1, giving it acceleration rights against a company we now own.
- The Buyer has no direct contractual relationship with Riverlark to compel the release.

This structure also leaves the "debt-free" price adjustment unanchored – if the release is post-Completion, what figure is deducted at Completion, and on what evidence?

**Push back:** Standard payoff mechanics: Seller to procure a payout letter from Riverlark dated no earlier than two Business Days before Completion; payout amount deducted from the Completion payment and paid directly to Riverlark at Completion; executed deeds of release and PPSR discharge forms delivered at Completion against receipt of funds. If the Seller insists on any post-Completion element, that requires (a) an irrevocable undertaking from Riverlark (not the Seller) to release on receipt of funds, and (b) Amelia Frost's written approval. Absent both, this is not acceptable.

### 2.10 DD-005 employee bonuses and funds flow (Disclosure Letter para 5)

| | Seller | Playbook |
|---|---|---|
| Treatment | "A matter for the Seller"; not itemised in funds flow | **AUD 420,000 plus triggered on-costs must be a specific line item or seller-funded; funds flow must not silently exclude them** |

**Analysis.** The Seller says the bonuses are "a matter for the Seller" but has not put them in the funds flow. That is internally inconsistent: if they are the Seller's cost, the funds flow should show a deduction from the Seller's proceeds; if they are not in the funds flow, the practical default is that the *target* pays them post-Completion – i.e., the Buyer bears them. The Seller's disclosure also expressly does not address superannuation, payroll tax or other on-costs, which could add materially to the AUD 420,000 headline.

Because the bonuses are conditional on Completion, they are a Completion-triggered liability of the target and fall squarely within what a debt-free/cash-free mechanism should capture.

**Push back:** Either (a) a specific line item in the Completion funds flow for AUD 420,000 plus all triggered superannuation, payroll tax and other on-costs, funded from the Seller's proceeds, or (b) the gross amount treated as Debt in the completion accounts. Require the Seller to confirm the on-cost figure. Also confirm whether the "continued employment" condition means any bonus falling away after Completion reverts to the Seller or the Buyer.

### 2.11 Ironquay IP (Clause 11.1; Disclosure Letter para 4)

| | Seller | Playbook |
|---|---|---|
| Indemnity scope | Limited to the SOW3 payment; "considered adequate" | **Broaden the indemnity, preserving the SOW3 cure; AUD 180,000 not independently verified either way** |

**Analysis.** The issue is not the AUD 180,000 – it is title to the SOW3 Project Materials. DD-004 clause 7.3 makes transfer of IP *conditional* on cleared payment of every SOW3 fee. If any fee is unpaid, Ironquay retains the IP. An indemnity limited to "the SOW3 payment" covers the Buyer for paying the invoice but not for the consequences of the target not owning IP it has presumably built product on: Ironquay licence/infringement claims, loss of use, re-development cost, customer impact, or a failed assignment even after payment.

The Seller's own disclosure is careful here: DD-010's AUD 180,000 is "not independent bank verification of non-payment," and there is no receipt and no confirmatory assignment in the data room. So the position is genuinely unverified in both directions – and that uncertainty is itself the reason the indemnity needs to be broader.

**Push back:** Retain the SOW3 cure mechanism (Seller to pay any outstanding fee pre-Completion and deliver a confirmatory assignment from Ironquay). Broaden Clause 11.1 to indemnify the Buyer/target against all Loss arising from (i) any failure of title to the SOW3 Project Materials or other Ironquay deliverables, (ii) any claim by Ironquay in respect of ownership, licensing or use of those materials, and (iii) the cost of obtaining a confirmatory assignment post-Completion if not delivered. This indemnity should sit outside the general cap, basket and time limits.

### 2.12 DD-006 export/privacy incident (Clause 4.6 / Schedule 6; Disclosure Letter para 6)

| | Seller | Playbook |
|---|---|---|
| Characterisation | "Preliminary operational matter"; "not expected to be material" | **Preserve logs, investigate, require updates; assume no confirmed breach, harm, notification duty or numeric demand in either direction** |

**Analysis.** The Seller's disclosure is factually measured (~1,240 records; names, business emails, roles, timestamps; access and scope not established; notification question open). The characterisation in the Seller Update ("not expected to be material") goes further than the disclosure supports and should not be accepted as a warranty-qualifying statement.

Consistent with the playbook, we should **not** assume this is a notifiable data breach, and we should not be putting a price on it. But equally we should not allow it to be deemed disclosed and closed off. The information involved (business contacts) is at the lower end of sensitivity, but the volume is non-trivial and the access question is unresolved.

**Push back:**
- Pre-Completion covenants: preserve all logs and evidence; complete and document the investigation; provide written updates to the Buyer; make any notification determined to be required.
- Specific indemnity (uncapped by the general regime) for Loss arising from the DD-006 incident, so the Buyer is protected if it later crystallises into a regulatory or third-party claim – without either side having to agree now that it will.
- Delete "not expected to be material" from any operative text; it is Seller opinion, not disclosure.

### 2.13 Sandbar renewals (Disclosure Letter para 8)

| | Seller | Playbook |
|---|---|---|
| Characterisation | "Ordinary-course operating costs" | **Assess; no automatic Debt classification or price deduction** |

**Analysis.** Three renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate), split across DD-008 and DD-011 and to be read together for timing and scope. The Seller's disclosure expressly does not say whether each is unavoidable, terminable, accrued or ordinary course – which is at odds with the Seller Update's assertion that they *are* ordinary course.

The playbook is correct that these should not be reflexively treated as Debt or deducted. The relevant questions are: (i) are any of them already committed/accrued (in which case they may belong in working capital or Debt), (ii) are they above historical run-rate (in which case they are a normalisation/quality-of-earnings point), (iii) do they contain change-of-control or minimum-term provisions that the share sale triggers? The split across two documents suggests we should check whether the three renewals are in substance one arrangement that has been divided.

**Push back:** Request the underlying renewal documents and accrual treatment. Reserve position on classification pending that. No price deduction proposed at this stage; no agreement that they are ordinary course.

### 2.14 Tax / IP under the general regime

| | Seller | Playbook |
|---|---|---|
| Position | "Settled under the general regime" | **OPEN; separate categories; no unlimited liability, no resolution** |

**Analysis.** Tax and IP are not settled. The Seller is trying to fold them into the 20% / 18-month / AUD 250k-deductible package via the Clause 13 "all Claims" default. Both categories conventionally carry their own regime (tax in particular typically has a longer period tied to the assessment window). We should not accept the general regime, but equally the playbook does not authorise us to demand unlimited tax/IP liability.

**Push back:** Carve both out of the general regime expressly and mark the tax covenant/indemnity and IP warranty regimes as open for separate negotiation. Resist any drafting that resolves them by default.

### 2.15 Title evidence (Disclosure Letter para 10)

| | Seller | Playbook |
|---|---|---|
| Evidence | Company share register (DD-012) | **Independent title/ownership/encumbrance/authority evidence; DD-012 is a supplied internal source, not independent proof** |

**Analysis.** The Seller's own disclosure concedes the point: DD-012 "identifies the source relied on for title and does not state that the Buyer has completed its own verification." A share register maintained by the company whose shares are being sold, supplied by the seller of those shares, is not independent evidence. It also says nothing about encumbrances (PPSR, Riverlark's security), options or convertible instruments, or the Seller's own authority to sell.

This interlocks with 2.4 and 2.9: the Seller wants title warranties capped at 20% and time-barred at 18 months, wants the Riverlark security released after Completion, and offers only its own register as proof of title. Taken together, that is a weak title position.

**Push back:** Pre-Completion deliverables: current ASIC extract for the target; PPSR search (and release of any registrations, including Riverlark's); Seller board resolution and constitutional authority to sell; certificate of no options/convertibles/pre-emption rights; confirmation that the share register reconciles to ASIC records. Title warranties remain under the Fundamental regime at 100% / six years.

---

## 3. Items that are broadly acceptable or non-contentious

For completeness – these do not require significant push-back on the current record:

- **Office lease (DL para 7):** notification only, not landlord consent. Confirm the notification is given pre-Completion and obtain a copy. Low priority.
- **Mossvale (DL para 9):** restriction on assignment, not change of control. Confirm no implied change-of-control trigger in the contract. Low priority.
- **Disclosure Letter para 11 (Reservation):** this is a Seller protection but does not harm us; it confirms the Letter contains no agreed positions, which is consistent with our own view that nothing is settled.

---

## 4. Summary of recommendations

**Threshold:**
1. Reject the "FINAL / settled at principal level" characterisation in writing. Confirm no Amelia Frost authority has been given for any fallback.

**Hold firm – no fallback authorised or appropriate:**
2. **Fundamental/Title regime:** 100% cap, six years minimum, outside basket/de minimis/knowledge.
3. **Fraud carve-out:** express carve-out from all caps, baskets, time bars, exclusive remedy and non-reliance.
4. **Clause 13 "all Claims" default:** delete; limitations apply only where expressly stated.
5. **Clause 8.3 buyer-knowledge exclusion:** delete entirely.
6. **General disclosure (DL 1.1–1.2):** strike; specific fair disclosure only.
7. **Riverlark:** payoff at Completion from Completion funds with releases delivered; no post-Completion release without Riverlark irrevocable undertaking and Frost approval.
8. **Bluefen:** effective unconditional consent plus evidence of 11.3 conditions satisfied, as a CP; no consent-on-delivery.
9. **Title evidence:** independent ASIC/PPSR/authority deliverables.

**Counter at playbook opening position – fallbacks exist but require Frost written approval:**
10. **Cap:** 25% / AUD 6.0m (do not signal 20%).
11. **Claims period:** 24 months (do not signal 18).

**Counter at playbook position – no fallback stated:**
12. **Thresholds:** AUD 5,000 / AUD 50,000 / first-dollar recovery. Prioritise the tipping mechanism.

**Specific items:**
13. **DD-005 bonuses:** line item for AUD 420,000 plus on-costs, Seller-funded; obtain on-cost figure.
14. **Ironquay:** broaden indemnity to cover title failure and third-party claims; keep SOW3 cure; place outside general regime.
15. **DD-006 incident:** investigation/preservation/update covenants plus specific indemnity; delete "not expected to be material"; no assumption of breach or quantum either way.
16. **Sandbar:** request documents; reserve classification; no automatic deduction.
17. **Tax / IP:** carve out of general regime; mark open.

**Internal action:** Confirm with Amelia Frost that no fallback authority has been granted and that she is aware the Seller is asserting principal-level agreement. If the deal team wishes to deploy either fallback (cap or claims period) as a trade, obtain her written authority referencing this draft before any communication to the Seller.
